sentences.text: Rui found out about it because of a maths test.

The test was on a Friday and he had meant to work on the Thursday evening, and on the Friday morning he had not worked on it, and the reason he had not worked on it was that he could not account for the Thursday evening at all.
He could account for the afternoon.
He had come in at twenty past four, and there had been the business with the bicycle chain in the yard, and his aunt had rung and been on the phone about the wedding for a while.
He could account for the night: he had been in bed at half nine and had read for a bit and had heard the ten o'clock news through the floor.
Between those two there was nothing.
Not a blur.
Not the ordinary vagueness of an evening where you did not do much.
Nothing at all, in the way that there is nothing before you were born.
He sat in the maths test working out what he could do about the four questions he had not revised, and underneath that he was thinking: *where did Thursday go.* It happened again on the Sunday.

He noticed it the moment it happened, or rather the moment after — he was at the kitchen table with the light on and it was properly dark outside and the last thing he was certain of was standing at the back door looking at the sky going orange behind the depot.
He got up and went to the door and opened it and stood there.
It was cold.
It was black.
The depot lights were on.
There was no orange anywhere.

He went and asked his mother what time it was and she said quarter past seven without looking up, and Rui stood in the kitchen doorway holding on to the frame and doing arithmetic that would not come out.
He had lost an hour and ten minutes and he had lost it while awake, standing up, at a back door.
Over the following fortnight he kept a record, which is what he did with things.
He wrote down the last moment he was sure of and the first moment after, and by the end of November he had nine entries and they had a shape.
It was always the same hour.
Not the same clock time — the clock time moved, earlier and earlier as the month went on.
It was the hour when the light goes.
The last of it, the part where the sky has colour in it and the streetlights come on and everything outdoors turns the colour of a photograph of itself.
That hour, a dozen times, had not happened to him.
He asked his mother, carefully, whether he had been strange on the Sunday.

She said he had been perfectly normal, that he had helped with the potatoes and had been quite chatty about a boy at school called Duarte, and that she did not know why he was asking, and could he not stand in the doorway with the cold coming in.
